where: Section 2, bullet on separate buses, and Quiz Q3 answer
problem: The text credits plain Harvard organisation with delivering 'an instruction and its two operands' in one cycle, and the Q3 answer says 'the two data operand fetches travel on different buses'. Plain Harvard gives one program bus and one data bus, so only one data operand per cycle. Fetching two operands (coefficient and sample) in the same cycle needs a second data bus or dual-ported data memory, which DSPs add on top of Harvard. A student may write the loose version in an exam.
fix: Say: 'Separate program and data buses (Harvard organisation, see chapter 1.6) let an instruction fetch and a data fetch happen in the same cycle. DSPs extend this with a second data bus (sometimes called modified Harvard) so the coefficient h[k] and the sample x[n − k] both arrive in the same cycle.' Match the Q3 answer to this wording.

problem: 'An SoC puts a complete system, radio included, on one die' reads as a definition, so a student will think every SoC must contain a radio. Many SoCs (a display controller chip, a motor-control SoC) have no radio at all. Section 3 itself only says a phone SoC has one.
fix: 'An SoC puts a complete system on one die: CPU cores, memory controller and peripherals, and often a radio as well.' Keep the phone as the example, not the rule.

problem: The text gives 'an ARM Cortex-A in a phone' as the modern microprocessor example, but section 3 says the phone processor is an SoC. The same chip is used as an example of two different families, which confuses the very distinction the chapter draws.
fix: Use a clear standalone microprocessor example, such as a desktop x86 CPU with external DRAM, and note that the same Cortex-A core appears inside a phone SoC covered in section 3.
